Principles of economics
Scarcity and opportunity cost
What does anything really cost?
The value of the best alternative given up. The production possibilities frontier draws the trade-offs of a whole economy.
MRT = −dy/dx
Comparative advantage and trade
Why trade with someone who is worse at everything?
Each side specializes where its opportunity cost is lowest, and both gain.
Supply, demand, equilibrium
How do prices coordinate millions of separate decisions?
At the equilibrium price the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied; shocks shift the curves.
Q<sub>d</sub>(P) = Q<sub>s</sub>(P)
Elasticity
How strongly do quantities respond to prices?
The percentage response of quantity to a one percent change in price. It decides who bears a tax.
ε = (dQ/dP)(P/Q)
Surplus, taxes, price controls
What does a market intervention cost?
Surplus measures the gains from trade; taxes and price controls destroy part of it as deadweight loss.
Externalities and public goods
When does the market get it wrong?
When a cost or benefit falls outside the transaction, or no one can be excluded from a good.
Firms and market structure
How much does a firm produce, and does competition matter?
Competitive firms produce where price equals marginal cost; a monopolist restricts output.
P = MC
Measuring the economy
How big is the economy and how fast are prices rising?
GDP counts final output; price indices turn nominal values real; surveys count the unemployed.

Long-run growth
Why are some countries rich and others poor?
Capital per worker, skills, technology, and the institutions that let them accumulate.
Money and banks
What is money, and who creates it?
Banks create deposits when they lend; the central bank sets the base and the policy rate.
MV = PY
Short-run fluctuations
Why do recessions happen?
With sticky prices, swings in total spending move output and employment.
Fiscal and monetary policy
What can governments and central banks do about it?
Spending, taxes and interest rates shift aggregate demand, with lags and limits.

general equilibrium and welfare

Walrasian equilibrium is where microeconomics meets the rest of the degree. Long-run macro is a general-equilibrium model with time; trade theory is general equilibrium with two countries; public economics starts from the second welfare theorem’s promise that efficiency and redistribution can be separated, and from the fact that the lump-sum transfers it needs do not exist.
Preferences are continuous, convex and locally non-satiated; endowments are positive.
Then aggregate excess demand z(p) is continuous and homogeneous of degree zero in prices.
Local non-satiation gives Walras’ law: p · z(p) = {0} for every price vector.
Prices can be normalized to a simplex; a continuous map of the simplex into itself has a fixed point (Brouwer). At that point z(p*) = {0}: an equilibrium exists.
First welfare theorem: with local non-satiation every Walrasian equilibrium is Pareto efficient.
Second welfare theorem: with convexity every Pareto-efficient allocation is an equilibrium after lump-sum transfers (separating hyperplane theorem).
from individuals to aggregates

Macroeconomics talks about one consumption function and one production function for a whole economy. Whether that is legitimate is a theorem, not a convenience, and the answer explains why most macro models have a single representative household.
Market demand is the sum of individual demands.
Individual demand obeys the Slutsky restrictions; summed demand generally does not.
Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu: aggregate excess demand inherits only continuity, homogeneity and Walras’ law, so equilibrium need not be unique or stable.
A representative agent exists exactly when preferences have the Gorman form, with linear and parallel Engel curves.
Heterogeneous-agent models are the modern response.
the Euler equation

Take the consumer from micro, date the goods, and the tangency becomes the most reused equation in the degree: consumption smoothing in macro, the IS curve of the three-equation model, asset prices in finance, the current account in international finance, and Ricardian equivalence in public finance.
A household maximizes Σ β<sup>t</sup> u(c<sub>t</sub>) subject to a lifetime budget: the two-good problem with goods dated t and t + {0}.
The price of tomorrow’s consumption in today’s is {0}/({1} + r).
The tangency becomes u′(c<sub>t</sub>) = β({0} + r)E[u′(c<sub>t+{1}</sub>)].
Consumption is smoothed: temporary income is spread over a lifetime (permanent income).
Log-linearized, it is the IS curve of the New Keynesian model.
Under uncertainty the same condition prices any asset: E[m R] = {0}.
production and distribution

The firm from micro, multiplied across an economy, becomes the aggregate production function, and the same marginal-product conditions that set a firm’s hiring set the shares of national income going to labor and capital.
A firm hires each factor until its marginal product equals its real price: w = F<sub>L</sub>, r = F<sub>K</sub>.
With constant returns, Euler’s theorem gives F(K, L) = F<sub>K</sub>K + F<sub>L</sub>L: factor payments exhaust output.
Aggregated, the economy has Y = F(K, AL); accumulating K gives the Solow model.
Growth accounting splits output growth into capital, labor and the residual, technology.
In an open economy, goods prices move factor prices (Stolper–Samuelson), so trade redistributes income.
strategic interaction

Once agents affect each other directly, the price-taking model of micro gives way to games, and the same equilibrium idea organizes oligopoly, central-bank credibility, trade wars and climate treaties.
A game lists players, strategies and payoffs.
A Nash equilibrium is a profile in which each strategy is a best response to the others.
Mixed strategies guarantee existence, again by a fixed-point theorem (Kakutani).
In dynamic games, subgame perfection discards threats that would not be carried out.
A central bank that cannot commit plays a dynamic game with the public, and ends with higher inflation for no gain (Kydland–Prescott).
information and incentives
Drop the assumption that everyone knows the same things and a new set of failures appears. The tools that handle them run through labor markets, banking, insurance and development.
Expected utility describes choice over risky prospects; concave utility is risk aversion.
Hidden types (adverse selection): the uninformed side’s best response can drive good types out of the market.
Signaling and screening: the informed take costly actions that reveal their type.
Hidden actions (moral hazard): contracts trade insurance against incentives.
Banks that fund illiquid loans with demand deposits can suffer self-fulfilling runs.
market failure and the state

Every assumption of the first welfare theorem names a field: missing markets lead to environmental economics, public goods to public finance, market power to industrial organization, and information to the economics of contracts.
The first welfare theorem needs complete markets, price taking and no externalities.
An externality is a missing market for a side effect, so marginal social and private costs diverge.
A tax equal to marginal external cost, tradable permits, or bargaining with clear property rights can restore efficiency.
Public goods require Σ MRS = MRT; voluntary contributions fall short.
If one distortion cannot be removed, removing another need not help (the theory of the second best).
money, interest rates and the exchange rate
The price level, the interest rate and the exchange rate are one system. Money and banking, monetary policy and international finance each study one face of it.
Quantity equation: MV = PY; in the long run money is neutral.
Fisher: the nominal rate is the real rate plus expected inflation.
With sticky prices, moving the nominal rate moves the real rate, which is how monetary policy works.
Open the economy: uncovered interest parity ties interest rates to expected depreciation.
Hence the trilemma: a fixed rate with free capital flows forces i = i*.
Every empirical field rests on the same question: what variation in the data identifies a causal effect? The answers taught in econometrics reappear, almost word for word, in the field courses.
OLS recovers a causal effect only if E[ε | X] = {0}.
Omitted variables, simultaneity and measurement error all violate it.
An instrument z, correlated with x but not with ε, identifies β = Cov(z, y)/Cov(z, x).
Differences-in-differences identifies an effect if treated and control groups would have moved in parallel.
Randomization makes treatment independent of everything else by design.
